Q: How do I debug a Mithril app in Visual Studio code A:

Welcome to JS + Mithril! You can absolutely debug your client-side Mithril app in Visual Studio Code using its built-in JavaScript debugger. Below are two simple ways—pick the one that matches how you set things up after Step 4 of the Mithril install guide.

Option A — “No bundler” (CDN script in index.html)

If you just have an index.html that loads Mithril via <script src="https://unpkg.com/mithril/mithril.js"></script> and your own app.js:

  1. Serve your files (browsers won’t allow file:// debugging nicely):

    • Quickest: open VS Code terminal and run:

      npx http-server . -p 5173

      (or use the “Live Server” extension; any localhost server is fine)

  2. Add a debug configuration:

    • In VS Code: Run & Debug → create a launch.json → choose Chrome (or Edge).

    • Use something like:

      {
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "Debug Chrome (localhost)",
      "type": "pwa-chrome",
      "request": "launch",
      "url": "http://localhost:5173/index.html",
      "webRoot": "${workspaceFolder}"
    }
  ]
}

  3. Set breakpoints in your own JS files (e.g., app.js) and press F5.

    • The browser opens and VS Code will hit your breakpoints.

    • If your code is in subfolders, ensure webRoot points to the folder that maps to / on your dev server.

Tip: If using <script type="module" src="./app.js"></script>, you’ll get nicer stack traces and breakpoints.

Option B — With a dev server (Vite/Parcel/Webpack)

If you prefer a modern setup (fast reload, source maps):

  1. Scaffold & run (Vite example):

    npm create vite@latest mithril-demo -- --template vanilla
cd mithril-demo
npm i mithril
npm run dev

    Then import Mithril in your code:

    import m from "mithril";
// ... your components/routes

  2. Debug via JavaScript Debug Terminal (zero config):

    • In VS Code: Run & Debug → JavaScript Debug Terminal.

    • Inside that terminal run npm run dev.

    • Open the URL it prints (e.g., http://localhost:5173). VS Code auto-attaches; set breakpoints and they’ll hit.

    OR use a launch config:

    {
  "version": "0.2.0",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "Launch Chrome (Vite)",
      "type": "pwa-chrome",
      "request": "launch",
      "url": "http://localhost:5173",
      "webRoot": "${workspaceFolder}"
    }
  ]
}

Vite (and similar) generates source maps by default, so breakpoints in your source files “just work.”

Common gotchas

  • Grey (hollow) breakpoints: VS Code can’t map them—make sure you’re serving from http://localhost:* and webRoot maps to the right folder. For bundlers, keep default source maps enabled.

  • Minified / CDN code: you can step into Mithril’s code, but you’ll mostly want breakpoints in your files.

  • Cache issues: Hard-reload the browser (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+R) when breakpoints don’t bind after edits.

Minimal example (no bundler)

index.html

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head><meta charset="utf-8" /><title>Mithril Debug</title></head>
  <body>
    <div id="app"></div>
    <script src="https://unpkg.com/mithril/mithril.js"></script>
    <script type="module" src="./app.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>

app.js

// Set a breakpoint on the next line
const Home = { view: () => m("div", "Hello Mithril!") };

m.mount(document.getElementById("app"), Home);

Serve (npx http-server -p 5173), press F5 with the launch config—done.

If you’re actually using Visual Studio (full .NET IDE) instead of VS Code, you’d typically launch Chrome/Edge and use the browser devtools, or attach the VS JavaScript debugger to a running browser instance; but the setup is much smoother in VS Code with the configs above.

Q: How to fix terminal hanging in Google Antigravity on Windows after command approval? A:

Root Cause

The issue occurs because on Windows, the agent sends commands to the terminal but does not send/detect the EOF (End of File) signal when the process finishes. This keeps the IDE in a "listening" loop, waiting for output that will never come.

Fix 1 — Add a Global Rule (Permanent Solution)

Go to Settings → Global Rules (or your .antigravityrules / .cursorrules file at the root of your project) and add the following instruction:

ENV: Windows.
Always use 'cmd /c' for all shell executions to ensure the process terminates
correctly and sends an EOF signal.

Example: Use 'cmd /c pip list' instead of just 'pip list'.

Avoid interactive shells. If a persistent session is needed, use 'cmd /k'
but ensure the command is self-terminating.

Why cmd /c works:

  • cmd /c runs the specified command and immediately terminates the shell process
  • This termination event is the signal Antigravity needs to unlock the chat UI
  • Without it, the shell remains "open" and the IDE waits forever

Why cmd /k is an alternative (not preferred):

  • cmd /k keeps the terminal window open after execution — good for viewing output, but the background process stays alive
  • Use it only when you need a persistent view; the background process can be closed manually

Fix 2 — Handle "Context Drift" (When AI Forgets the Rule)

After long conversations, the agent may "forget" the Global Rule. This is a known behavior called context drift. When the terminal starts hanging again mid-session, use one of these nudges in the chat:

Situation What to Type
Agent forgot the rule "Follow global rules: use cmd /c"
Quick reminder "Remember cmd /c"
Force re-run "Rerun that using cmd /c so it terminates properly"

Verification — Test Commands

After applying the Global Rule, test it with these commands:

"List all installed Python packages"
→ Agent should run: cmd /c pip list

"Check internet connection 4 times"  
→ Agent should run: cmd /c ping google.com -n 4

"Show OS version info"
→ Agent should run: cmd /c systeminfo | findstr /B /C:"OS Name" /C:"OS Version"

✅ Success indicators:

  • Output appears in chat
  • "Running..." status changes to a checkmark or disappears
  • You can type a new prompt immediately without pressing Stop

Q: "yum -y install nfs-utils nfs-utils-lib" when installing NFS client on a CentOS vagrant machine A:

There was a bug in the CentOS 7 - packages that caused this error:

When updating only device-mapper subpackages, without updating lvm2 package, we may have ended up with file conflicts if files were moved around subpackages. ... To avoid problems when updating from older versions, there's direct conflict defined explicitly in the packages now which, if hit, will give an information about the minimum required version to resolve this conflict.

So, updating lvm2 is a solution. I think that yum update solved the problem because the conflict that was added to the packages was loaded from the package repository as part of the package information. So, lvm2 was probably updated when device-mapper was installed by Vagrant and this update avoids the error.
